title: Persistent Prayer, Humble Faith, and the Cost of Following
summary: Jesus tells a parable of a widow who wears down an unjust judge, to teach persistence in prayer, and a parable of a Pharisee and a tax collector at prayer, in which the humble sinner goes home justified. He welcomes infants, tells a wealthy ruler to sell everything and follow him, and for the third time predicts his death and resurrection. Near Jericho he gives sight to a blind beggar who calls him Son of David.
story:
The chapter continues directly from the warning about the day of the Son of Man at the end of chapter 17. If that day may be long in coming, disciples need to keep praying and not lose heart, and Jesus asks whether he will find faith on earth when he comes (verse 8). The rest of the chapter answers the question of who enters the kingdom. Not the self-assured Pharisee but the tax collector who begs for mercy. Not the ruler who has kept the commandments but cannot let go of his wealth, but those who receive the kingdom like an infant. Not the disciples who hear the plainest prediction of the cross and understand none of it (verse 34), but, for the moment, a blind beggar who sees who Jesus is.

Luke has been following his own path through Jesus' teaching since 9:51, with much material found only in his Gospel. At verse 15 he rejoins the order of Mark (Mark 10:13-52), though he passes over Mark's story of James and John asking for the best seats (Mark 10:35-45), which he echoes later at the Last Supper (22:24-27). The third reminder that Jesus is going up to Jerusalem (verse 31) brings the long road near its end: Jesus draws near Jericho, the last stop before the climb to the city, and in chapter 19 he meets Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector who shows what the rich ruler could not.
historical:
The temple in Jerusalem, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great from about 20/19 BC, was the center of Jewish worship. A lamb was offered as the daily whole burnt offering (the Tamid) every morning and afternoon (Exodus 29:38-42; m. Tamid), and the afternoon offering, at about three o'clock, was also an hour of public prayer, when incense was burned and people gathered to pray (Luke 1:10, Acts 3:1). Individuals also came up to pray on their own. Kenneth Bailey (Through Peasant Eyes, 1980) argued that the parable pictures the two men at the atonement sacrifice, which would give the tax collector's plea for atonement (verse 13) its setting; the parable does not say so, but it places them both ‘in the temple’ where sacrifice was offered.

The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to the exact keeping of the Law as interpreted by their traditions. Josephus calls them the most accurate interpreters of the laws (Jewish War 2.162), says they handed down practices from the fathers not written in the Law of Moses (Antiquities 13.297), and reports that they were highly regarded by ordinary people, whose prayers and worship followed the Pharisees' teaching (Antiquities 18.15). The Pharisee in the parable represents the most admired kind of piety of his day. Tax collectors in Judea and Galilee were local men who collected tolls and taxes for Roman authorities or Herodian rulers, often by contracting for the right and keeping what they could take above the required amount. They were widely regarded as collaborators and cheats, and the Mishnah later grouped them with murderers and robbers (m. Nedarim 3:4).

Jewish towns had local courts, and under Roman rule some cases also went before officials appointed by Herodian rulers or Rome. The Law's charge to judges was to judge fairly and take no bribes (Deuteronomy 16:18-20), and King Jehoshaphat told his judges to let the fear of the LORD be on them (2 Chronicles 19:6-7). The prophets condemned judges who would not take up the widow's cause (Isaiah 1:23). A judge who neither fears God nor respects people fails both duties at once.

Jericho lay about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem, near the Jordan, some 800 feet below sea level, while Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet above it, so the road up climbed over 3,000 feet through the desert (the setting of the parable of the good Samaritan, 10:30). It was the usual starting point for pilgrims coming from Galilee by the Jordan valley, and at Passover the road would be crowded. New Testament Jericho was a Hasmonean and Herodian city of winter palaces and gardens beside the Wadi Qelt, a short distance from the ancient mound of the older city (Tell es-Sultan); its palaces were excavated by Ehud Netzer from the 1970s. Herod the Great died there in 4 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 17). Mark places the healing of blind Bartimaeus as Jesus was leaving Jericho (Mark 10:46), and Matthew has two blind men as he left (Matthew 20:29-34), while Luke has one man as Jesus was approaching the city. Calvin (Harmony of the Gospels, 1555) suggested that the man began crying out as Jesus approached and was healed as he left; others point to the old and new sites lying side by side; many scholars think Luke simply rearranged the story so that the Zacchaeus episode could follow inside the city.
cultural:
Widows in the ancient world were often without a male protector to argue their case in court, and the Law repeatedly commands justice for the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 10:18, 24:17). The wisdom book of Sirach, from the early second century BC, says that the Lord does not ignore the widow's supplication when she pours out her complaint, and that he will not delay or be patient with her oppressors (Sirach 35, verses 14-22 or 17-22 depending on the edition), language that Luke 18:7 closely echoes. Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014) cautions against assuming every widow was poor and powerless: this one has an adversary, pursues her case relentlessly, and asks the judge to ‘avenge’ her (ekdikeō), and the judge fears she will literally give him a black eye (hupōpiazō, a boxing term, verse 5). The comedy of a powerful judge afraid of a persistent widow is part of the story's force.

The Pharisee's practices went beyond what the Law required. The Law commanded one annual fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29-31); some devout Jews fasted twice a week, and the early Christian manual called the Didache (8:1) says that ‘the hypocrites’ fast on Mondays and Thursdays and tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays instead. The Law required tithes of grain, wine, oil, and the firstborn of the herds (Deuteronomy 14:22-23); the Pharisee tithes everything he acquires, including purchased produce that the grower might not have tithed, a concern that fills the Mishnah's tractate Demai. His prayer is a thanksgiving, a recognized form of Jewish prayer: the Babylonian Talmud (b. Berakhot 28b) preserves a prayer of Rabbi Nehunya ben HaKanah on leaving the house of study, thanking God that his portion is with those who study rather than with those who sit in theaters and circuses. The Psalms also include protests of innocence (Psalm 17:3-5, 26:1-7). What Jesus targets is not thanksgiving but contempt: the Pharisee thanks God that he is not like ‘this tax collector’.

People normally prayed standing, often with raised eyes and hands (Psalm 123:1, 1 Timothy 2:8). The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes, and beats his breast, a gesture of grief and contrition that Luke mentions again at the cross (23:48). Parents brought children to revered teachers for blessing, as Jacob laid his hands on Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:14). Luke calls them brephē, ‘infants’, where Mark says children (Mark 10:13), sharpening the point that they bring nothing. The ruler (archōn) may have been a synagogue leader or member of a local council; he is ‘extremely wealthy’ (verse 23). In the camel saying, the camel was the largest animal in the region and the needle's eye the smallest opening, a deliberate picture of impossibility; the Babylonian Talmud uses the image of an elephant passing through the eye of a needle for the same idea (b. Berakhot 55b, b. Bava Metzia 38b). The popular idea that a small gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye lies behind the saying has no ancient support and first appears in medieval writers. Cyril of Alexandria suggested that kamēlos (camel) should be read kamilos (rope), and a few late manuscripts have that reading, but the camel is original.

Blind beggars sat by roads where pilgrims passed, since almsgiving was a pious duty, especially near festivals. The blind man calls Jesus ‘Son of David’, the royal title of the promised king: the Psalms of Solomon, from the first century BC, pray for God to raise up the son of David as king over Israel (Psalms of Solomon 17:21). Dennis Duling (Solomon, Exorcism, and the Son of David, Harvard Theological Review 68, 1975) argued that the title in healing stories may also recall Solomon, David's son, whom later Jewish tradition remembered as a healer and exorcist (Josephus, Antiquities 8.45-49).
literary:
Luke frames both opening parables by telling the reader their point in advance (verses 1 and 9), an unusual feature. The two parables form a pair on prayer: one on persistence, one on humility. The first uses an inner speech, like the rich fool and the dishonest manager (12:17-19, 16:3-4), and argues from the lesser to the greater: if even an unjust judge gives in to persistence, how much more will God, who is just and loves his elect. Its application (verses 6-8) turns from the judge to God and then, unexpectedly, back to the disciples: the real question is not whether God will act but whether the Son of Man will find faith.

The second parable uses sharp contrast and reversal. Two men go up to the temple; one prays ‘to himself’ or ‘about himself’ and uses the first person five times in two verses, while the other stands far off and names himself ‘the sinner’. The verdict, that the tax collector ‘went down to his house justified rather than the other’, uses the verb dikaioō, which ties the parable back to 16:15, where Jesus told the Pharisees that they justify themselves before others, and to the lawyer who wanted to justify himself (10:29). The closing saying repeats 14:11: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

The scenes that follow pair two more figures, infants who bring nothing and a ruler who has everything. In both the disciples or the crowd get in the way: the disciples rebuke those bringing the babies (verse 15), and those leading the procession rebuke the blind man (verse 39), using the same verb (epitimaō), and both times Jesus calls for the one being turned away. The ruler's question, ‘what must I do to inherit eternal life?’, repeats the lawyer's in 10:25 almost word for word. Jesus' answer moves from the commandments to the one thing lacking, then to a saying about camels and needles, the disciples' dismay, and the reassurance that what is impossible for people is possible with God. The third passion prediction is the fullest in Luke, and it is followed by a threefold statement of the disciples' incomprehension (verse 34) found only here. The chapter closes with a blind man who sees who Jesus is, receives his sight, and follows him, while those who can see have not understood. The healing leads into Zacchaeus (19:1-10), and the words ‘followed’ and ‘glorifying God’ recall the call of the disciples (5:11) and the praise that greets Jesus' works throughout the Gospel.

outline.t: The widow and the unjust judge
The Pharisee and the tax collector
Receiving the kingdom like a child
The rich ruler and the cost of the kingdom
Jesus predicts his death and resurrection a third time
A blind beggar near Jericho receives his sight

doctrines.note: Jesus teaches that his people “need to pray at all times and not lose heart” (verse 1), because God is not like the unjust judge: he hears his elect who cry to him day and night. The second parable adds that God hears the prayer that pleads for mercy, not the one that reports its own merits.

The tax collector goes home justified, declared in the right with God, having brought nothing but confession and a plea for mercy (verses 13-14), while the man who trusted in his own righteousness (verse 9) does not. The parable shows in Jesus' own teaching the pattern Paul later sets out: God justifies the ungodly who trust him (Romans 4:5).

Wealth makes entering the kingdom humanly impossible (verses 24-25), not because money is evil but because it holds the heart, as it held the ruler who went away very sad (verse 23). Yet what is impossible with man is possible with God (verse 27), and those who leave everything receive far more (verses 29-30).

The blind man calls Jesus “Son of David” twice (verses 38-39), the title of the promised king, and Jesus accepts it. In the same chapter Jesus says that the Son of Man will be handed over, mocked, flogged, killed, and raised, as the prophets wrote (verses 31-33): the Messiah reigns through suffering.

Jesus asks whether the Son of Man will find faith on earth (verse 8), and the chapter answers in people: the persistent widow, the tax collector, the infants, and the blind man who calls out all the louder and hears, “Your faith has healed you” (verse 42).

words.note: Ekkakeō (also spelled enkakeō), to lose heart, grow weary, give up. It occurs six times in the New Testament, only here in the Gospels (verse 1); Paul uses it for not losing heart in ministry (2 Corinthians 4:1, 4:16) and not growing weary in doing good (Galatians 6:9, 2 Thessalonians 3:13). The parable is addressed to the temptation to stop praying when God seems slow.

Ekdikēsis, vindication, justice, and in other contexts punishment or vengeance. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, three in Luke (18:7, 18:8, 21:22), and the related verb ekdikeō, ‘give justice, avenge’, is the widow's plea (verses 3 and 5). Paul uses the noun in ‘Vengeance is Mine’ (Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35). Here it means God's righting of wrongs for those who have been wronged, a promise that leaves vengeance with God.

Hupōpiazō, literally to strike under the eye, give a black eye, and so to wear out or treat roughly. It occurs twice in the New Testament: here (verse 5) and in Paul's ‘I discipline my body’ (1 Corinthians 9:27), where it is a boxer's word. The judge's fear may be literal (she will hit him) or figurative (she will wear him out or blacken his reputation); either way the humor is intentional.

Exoutheneō, to despise, treat as nothing, look down on with contempt. It occurs 11 times in the New Testament, twice in Luke: in verse 9, of those who ‘viewed others with contempt’, and in 23:11, where Herod and his soldiers treat Jesus with contempt. Peter applies it to Jesus as the stone ‘rejected’ by the builders (Acts 4:11). The parable is aimed at the contempt as much as at the self-trust.

Hilaskomai, in the passive to be propitiated, to be merciful, and in the Septuagint to make atonement or forgive. It occurs only twice in the New Testament: in the tax collector's prayer, hilasthēti moi, ‘be propitiated toward me’ or ‘have mercy on me’ (verse 13), and in Hebrews 2:17, where Christ makes atonement for the sins of the people. The Septuagint uses it in Psalm 79:9 (78:9 in its numbering), ‘atone for our sins’. The related nouns hilastērion (Romans 3:25, Hebrews 9:5) and hilasmos (1 John 2:2, 4:10) belong to the language of atonement. C. H. Dodd (The Bible and the Greeks, 1935) argued for the sense ‘expiate’ (sin covered and removed), Leon Morris (The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross, 1955) for ‘propitiate’ (wrath turned aside); many see both. Standing where sacrifices were offered, the tax collector asks God to deal with his sin as only God can.

Dikaioō, to justify, to declare or show to be in the right. It occurs 39 times in the New Testament, 15 in Romans and 8 in Galatians, and five in Luke (7:29, 7:35, 10:29, 16:15, 18:14). In the Septuagint it is often a courtroom word for acquitting the innocent (Deuteronomy 25:1). Protestant and Roman Catholic traditions differ over whether justification is only God's verdict or also includes the renewal of the person, but all agree that here the verdict is God's and goes to the one who asked for mercy. The perfect participle, dedikaiōmenos, pictures him going home in a settled state of being justified.

Brephos, infant, unborn or newborn child. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, five of them in Luke: the unborn John leaping in Elizabeth's womb (1:41, 1:44), the baby lying in a manger (2:12, 2:16), and the infants brought to Jesus here (verse 15). Mark's parallel says paidia, ‘children’. Luke's word underlines that those whom Jesus says the kingdom belongs to can bring nothing and do nothing to earn it.

Anablepō, to look up, and to regain sight. It occurs 25 times in the New Testament, seven in Luke, three of them in this healing (verses 41, 42, 43). The related noun anablepsis, ‘recovery of sight’, appears in Jesus' reading of Isaiah 61 at Nazareth, where he says he was sent to proclaim “recovery of sight to the blind” (4:18). The healing at Jericho is that program carried out on the road to the cross.

christ:
The chapter's opening parable ends with the Son of Man's coming (verse 8), so that prayer in Luke is set within the hope of his return. The God who will vindicate his elect is the Father to whom Jesus himself prays at every turning point in this Gospel, and whose justice will be shown when the Son of Man comes.

The tax collector's prayer, ‘be propitiated toward me, the sinner’, asks for what the Christian gospel says God provided in Christ. Hebrews uses the same verb for Christ as the high priest who makes atonement for the sins of the people (Hebrews 2:17), and Paul calls Christ the hilastērion, the mercy seat or place of atonement, displayed in his blood (Romans 3:25). Luke does not draw that line within the parable, but the chapter itself turns from the temple, where the tax collector stands at a distance, to the road where Jesus announces that he will be handed over, mocked, spit upon, flogged, and killed (verses 32-33), language that recalls the Servant who gave his back to those who struck him and did not hide his face from spitting (Isaiah 50:6) and was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, quoted at 22:37). He says that everything the prophets wrote about the Son of Man will be fulfilled (verse 31), a theme Luke brings to its climax when the risen Christ opens the Scriptures (24:25-27, 24:44-47).

The ruler calls him ‘Good Teacher’, and Jesus replies, “Why do you call Me good?” and adds, “No one is good except God alone” (verse 19). Readers have taken this in different ways: as Jesus deflecting a flattering title, as a challenge to the ruler to consider what he is really saying, or as a sign of the Son's humility before the Father. Arian writers in the fourth century used it to argue that the Son is less than God, and the fathers who answered them read it as a question meant to lead the ruler to recognize God in Jesus. What the passage plainly shows is that Jesus claims the authority to add to the commandments a call to follow him (verse 22), and that eternal life is found in that following.

The blind man twice calls Jesus Son of David, the royal title of the Messiah promised to David's line (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and Jesus does not silence him. Jesus is about to enter Jerusalem as king (19:38). He heals as the one anointed to give recovery of sight to the blind (4:18, Isaiah 61:1 in its Greek form, and compare Isaiah 35:5), and the healed man follows him. The church confesses this Jesus as the Son of David according to the flesh and the Son of God in power (Romans 1:3-4), crucified, risen on the third day, and coming again.
interpretation:
The persistent widow was read by the fathers as a model of perseverance in prayer. Augustine's Letter 130, written to the widow Proba in 412, uses Luke 18:1 to teach that praying always means a continual desire for God sustained by faith, hope, and love, alongside set times of spoken prayer. Medieval and Reformation preachers made the parable a call to importunate prayer, sometimes applying it to the church's cry for justice under persecution. Modern interpreters debate whether the widow stands for the praying believer (the traditional view) or whether, as Amy-Jill Levine (2014) argues, a parable about a vengeful widow and a co-opted judge resists being domesticated into a lesson on prayer; Luke's own framing (verse 1) and application (verses 6-8) take it as the former. The Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read verses 1-8 in October of Year C.

The Pharisee and the tax collector became a central text for the doctrine of grace. The Reformers read it as a picture of justification by faith apart from works. In Lutheran Leipzig verses 9-14 were the Gospel for the Eleventh Sunday after Trinity: Bach's solo cantata Mein Herze schwimmt im Blut (BWV 199) was performed on that Sunday in Weimar in 1714, and Siehe zu, daß deine Gottesfurcht nicht Heuchelei sei (BWV 179, 1723) and Herr Jesu Christ, du höchstes Gut (BWV 113, 1724) followed in Leipzig. Søren Kierkegaard wrote a communion discourse on the tax collector (Three Discourses at the Communion on Fridays, 1849). In the Orthodox churches the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee opens the Lenten Triodion, the season of preparation for Lent. The tax collector's prayer, joined to the blind man's cry ‘Son of David, have mercy on me’ (verse 38), stands behind the Jesus Prayer (‘Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner’), the prayer of the Orthodox hesychast tradition made widely known by the nineteenth-century Russian The Way of a Pilgrim. Modern scholarship since E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) has stressed that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation by works, and Levine proposed that the phrase para ekeinon (verse 14) might even mean that the tax collector was justified ‘alongside’ or ‘because of’ the Pharisee, a reading most commentators think the grammar and the reversal saying rule out.

The blessing of the children was cited on both sides of the baptism debate. Tertullian (On Baptism 18) quoted ‘forbid them not’ but counseled delaying baptism until children could know Christ, while Calvin (Institutes 4.16.7) used the passage to argue for infant baptism, and Mark's parallel was read in the Book of Common Prayer's service of infant baptism. Baptists and other believer-baptist traditions reply that the passage speaks of blessing, not baptism.

The rich ruler prompted Clement of Alexandria's treatise Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (about AD 200), which reads Mark's version as a call to inner detachment rather than literal poverty. Athanasius tells how Antony of Egypt heard Matthew's form of the command read in church and gave away his inheritance (Life of Antony 2), a founding story of monasticism, and Francis of Assisi built his order on the same call. Heinrich Hofmann's painting Christ and the Rich Young Ruler (1889) hangs in the Riverside Church in New York. In Lutheran use verses 31-43 were the Gospel for Estomihi, the Sunday before Lent, for which Bach wrote his two Leipzig audition cantatas of 1723, Jesus nahm zu sich die Zwölfe (BWV 22) and Du wahrer Gott und Davids Sohn (BWV 23), and later Herr Jesu Christ, wahr' Mensch und Gott (BWV 127) and Sehet, wir gehn hinauf gen Jerusalem (BWV 159, 1729). The Orthodox read verses 18-27 and 35-43 on the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Sundays of Luke.
text:
A few differences between manuscripts and translations affect English Bibles. In verse 11 the phrase pros heauton can go with ‘stood’ (‘stood by himself’, BSB, NIV) or with ‘prayed’ (‘prayed thus with himself’, King James Version; ‘prayed about himself’), and the manuscripts differ in word order, some placing ‘these things’ before and some after it. In verse 14 the earliest manuscripts read par' ekeinon, ‘rather than that one’, while later Byzantine manuscripts phrase the comparison differently; the sense is the same. In verse 24 the words ‘having become very sad’ are missing from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and a few other early witnesses, and some editions omit them; the BSB's “Seeing the man's sadness” reflects the longer text.

In verse 29 Luke's list of what disciples have left includes ‘wife’, which Mark's parallel does not have (Mark 10:29); later copyists added it to some manuscripts of Matthew 19:29. In verse 25 a few late manuscripts read kamilon, ‘rope’, instead of kamēlon, ‘camel’; all early witnesses have camel. Verse 20 lists the commandments in the order adultery, murder, theft, the order also found in the Nash Papyrus (a Hebrew text of the Ten Commandments from about the second century BC), in Codex Vaticanus of the Septuagint, in Philo, and in Romans 13:9 and James 2:11, while the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Mark 10:19 put murder first.

teach.big: The kingdom is received, not earned: by those who keep crying to God, who plead for mercy rather than cite their merits, who come with empty hands, who let go of what holds them, and who see in the crucified Son of David the one to follow.

outline.t: Pray and do not lose heart; even an unjust judge yields to persistence.
God is not like the judge: he will vindicate his people, and the real question is whether we will keep faith until the Son of Man comes.
Trust in one's own righteousness breeds contempt for others and turns prayer into self-report.
God justifies the one who pleads for mercy, and he humbles the self-exalted.
The kingdom belongs to those who, like infants, receive it with nothing to offer.
Keeping the commandments cannot replace following Jesus, and whatever we will not give up for him has become our master.
Salvation is impossible for people and possible with God, and no one who leaves anything for the kingdom loses.
Jesus goes to Jerusalem to suffer and rise as the prophets wrote, though even his friends do not yet understand.
A blind beggar sees what others miss, cries for mercy, receives sight, and follows Jesus in praise.

teach.pitfalls:
The widow and the judge is misread when God is pictured as a reluctant judge who must be nagged into acting. The parable argues by contrast: if even an unjust judge yields, how much more will a just and loving God. Nor does it promise that persistent prayer obtains anything we ask; it promises that God will vindicate his people and asks whether we will keep faith.

The Pharisee and the tax collector is often preached in a way that reproduces the Pharisee's error: listeners thank God they are not like that Pharisee. The parable turns on anyone who trusts in their own righteousness and despises others, and it catches religious people of every kind. Avoid caricaturing Pharisees or first-century Judaism as a religion of earning salvation; the Pharisee here was admired, and his practices were sincere (see the first hard question). Avoid also making the tax collector a model of low self-esteem or implying that his sin did not matter; he names himself a sinner and asks for atonement, and Zacchaeus in the next chapter shows repentance at work.

On verses 15-17, do not load the passage with a settled answer to the infant baptism debate; it has been used on both sides. On the rich ruler, do not dissolve the command into a mere attitude test, and do not turn it into a universal rule that every disciple must sell everything (see the second hard question). The needle's-eye gate story should be dropped from teaching; it has no basis and softens a saying meant to be impossible. On Jericho, do not hide the differences between the Gospels or force them; state them honestly.
teach.pastoral: The parable of the widow will press on people who have prayed for years without the answer they sought: for a healing, a child's return, a marriage, or justice after abuse or wrong. Honor that pain. The text does not promise that every request will be granted as asked; it promises that God hears and will vindicate, and it names losing heart as a real danger. Do not suggest that unanswered prayer means too little faith. For those seeking justice after abuse or crime, the widow's refusal to be silent is a word of dignity; keep a path to real help open, including the authorities and qualified advocates. The tax collector's prayer is good news for the scrupulous, those who fear they have never repented enough; he is justified by God's mercy, not by the quality of his contrition. And the call to the rich ruler must be preached to the comfortable without crushing those who are already poor, for whom the promise of verses 29-30 and the welcome of the infants and the beggar are the chapter's word.

hard.q: Does the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector caricature Pharisees and Judaism?
hard.a:
The objection is strong and has been pressed by Jewish and Christian scholars alike. Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014; with Ben Witherington III, The Gospel of Luke, 2018) argues that Christian preaching has turned the Pharisee into a symbol of Jewish legalism and hypocrisy, so that the parable teaches contempt for Jews, the very contempt it condemns. E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) showed that the Judaism of the period understood Israel's place in the covenant as God's gracious gift, with obedience as the response, not as a means of earning salvation, a pattern he called covenantal nomism. Luke's own framing, that Jesus told the parable to those who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt (verse 9), has been read by some critics as a Christian sharpening of the story against the Pharisees. And the Pharisee's thanksgiving has close parallels in admired Jewish prayers (b. Berakhot 28b) and in the Psalms.

Responses begin with what the text does and does not say. Luke does not say that Pharisees as such trusted in themselves; verse 9 names a kind of person, not a group. The Pharisee's practices are presented as real and costly, and Jesus does not mock them. Luke also shows Pharisees inviting Jesus to meals (7:36, 11:37, 14:1), warning him of danger (13:31), and in Acts Gamaliel counseling restraint (Acts 5:34-39) and Paul still calling himself a Pharisee (Acts 23:6). The target of the parable is contempt and self-trust, sins that the prophets and the rabbis also condemned, and the story's reversal falls on Christian readers who thank God they are not like the Pharisee. Many Christian commentators accept much of the historical correction while holding that the parable's point, that God justifies the one who pleads for mercy, stands. Most interpreters today agree that the parable must be taught without caricature; they differ on how much Luke's framing shapes it.

hard.q: Must every follower of Jesus sell everything, as the rich ruler was told?
hard.a:
Some readers insist that the command means exactly what it says for everyone. Many monastic traditions, from Antony of Egypt onward, and radical movements from the Franciscans to some Anabaptist communities, have taken it as a real call to renounce possessions; Luke himself records that the early church in Jerusalem held everything in common (Acts 2:44-45, 4:32-35) and that Jesus told disciples to sell their possessions and give alms (12:33) and that none can be his disciple without renouncing all (14:33). The second-century satirist Lucian (The Passing of Peregrinus 13) mocked Christians for despising possessions and holding them in common, which shows how visible the practice once was; modern critics, inside and outside the church, have noted how seldom it has been followed since, and some argue that the easier interpretations were invented to spare the rich. The command should not be softened into a suggestion.

Other interpreters point out that Luke does not present it as a rule for every disciple. In the next chapter Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor and repays fourfold those he cheated, and Jesus declares that salvation has come to his house (19:8-9); Luke mentions women who supported Jesus from their own means (8:3); and in Acts the sharing of property is voluntary (Acts 5:4). Clement of Alexandria (Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?) argued that Jesus demands the renunciation of the passions and attachments wealth breeds. Many Reformation and modern interpreters conclude that Jesus diagnosed the particular thing that held this man and demanded its surrender because it stood between him and following. Roman Catholic teaching distinguishes the precepts binding all from the counsels of perfection (poverty, chastity, obedience) to which some are called, a distinction Protestants have often criticized. What no reading can escape is the principle: whatever a person will not give up for Jesus has become a rival to him, wealth is named as an especially powerful rival, and Jesus promises that no one who leaves home or family for the kingdom will fail to receive far more.
